Saudi Arabia said Tuesday it had intercepted a drone targeting Riyadh, as well as a missile it previously said was taken down.
Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, said on X that a drone had also been intercepted and destroyed, without specifying who was believed to have launched it.
The bulletin came after the country's Civil Defense said earlier that people in the Riyadh area should "avoid crowds or going to dangerous areas, and refrain from taking photos" in a post on X , before saying the danger had passed .
Shortly after, Al-Maliki said a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis at Riyadh had been " intercepted and destroyed ."
French President Emmanuel Macron has secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain during a tour of the Persian Gulf, the French presidency said Tuesday.
He obtained commitments for around 100,000 tons per month from the UAE, and an additional 100,000 tons from Bahrain, the French Elysee presidential palace said, according to the AFP news agency.
With the addition of deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France has commitments for 295,000 tons per month, representing just over 10% of its consumption, the statement added.
Macron is undertaking a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf in an effort to secure oil and diesel and bring down prices in France after a weekend of violent protests over soaring living costs and other social issues.
The G7 countries, chaired this year by France, agreed in early October to release up to 100 million barrels of oil from their strategic reserves to ease pressure on global fuel supplies amid the U.S.-Iran war.
The shipments for France will be sent overland via Oman, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, the French presidency said. Experts have questioned whether the deliveries will have an impact on prices in France, however, given the risk of renewed fighting in the region.
Iran's Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces warned Tuesday that Tehran would not wait for the U.S. midterm elections before retaliating to any new U.S. attack.
Maj. Gen. Abdollahi said Iran "has not waited, nor will it wait, for the results of the U.S. congressional elections" to respond to any new attack.
He blamed regional insecurity on the presence of U.S. forces and warned countries hosting American troops to remain vigilant.
"Countries hosting the United States in the region should also know that the main cause of insecurity in the region is the presence of the terrorist U.S. military," he said.
The U.K. government announced Tuesday that it is expanding military support for Saudi Arabia as it faces ongoing attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, including "defensive" air patrols by British Royal Air Force jets over the kingdom.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Royal Air Force Typhoon jets would "conduct defensive counter-air operations over Saudi Arabia, helping to protect Saudi cities, civilian populations and critical national infrastructure from Houthi attack."
He said British planes would not strike Houthi targets in Yemen.
The U.K. will also send a military transport plane and an unspecified number of military advisers to Saudi Arabia, Streeting said.
The announcement follows Britain's decision last month to offer in-air refueling of Saudi planes operating against the Iran-backed rebels. That mission is being extended by another 90 days, Streeting said.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a government military camp in southern Yemen rose to 73 people Tuesday, making it the deadliest strike since fighting in the country began escalating three months ago, a senior Yemeni government official said Tuesday.
The recruits were all aged between 18 and 20, and some were still missing a day after the Iran-backed Houthis hit the al-Alam camp in the southern province of Shabwa with ballistic missiles, according to provincial governor Awad Ibn al-Wazir.
Negotiations between Iran and the United States are ongoing despite rising tension and repeated statements from President Trump that the U.S. could resume major strikes on Iran next month, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said Tuesday.
"The negotiation is ongoing. We are seeing engagement from the parties," al-Ansari, who also serves as an adviser to Qatar's prime minister, said at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday.
Al-Ansari did not offer any further information on the negotiations, including whether there have been any recent direct contacts between Iranian and U.S. officials or if the talks are being conducted entirely via mediators.
He said discussions were continuing with regional partners and expressed hope that diplomatic efforts would eventually lead to an agreement, while cautioning that conditions on the ground were becoming increasingly difficult.
"Escalation left unchecked will mean that we are spiraling towards a regional war that will expand beyond the borders of our region," he warned.

Iran's military said Tuesday morning that it had destroyed another U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone and attacked two more tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires on the unnamed ships.
In a statement, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have struck and destroyed an MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz.
At least 24 American MQ-9 Reapers, two MQ-1 drones and an MQ-4C Triton have been lost since the U.S. began its war with Iran, representing a loss of more than $800  million, according to a report released by the Congressional Budget Office in September.
The IRGC also claimed two oil tankers trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iran's permission, using a southern route endorsed by the Trump administration but not recognized by Tehran, were hit by sea mines laid by the IRGC, forcing them to halt due to fires on board.
Iran has routinely targeted vessels in and near the strait for months, challenging Trump administration assertions that the vital shipping lanes are open to commercial traffic and that the U.S. military has complete control of the waterway.
At the end of August, President Trump himself declared the strait mine-free , saying U.S. forces had "totally cleared the strait of mines … Any boat goes through with a mine, we take it out."
The U.S. Navy has also struck vessels in the region as part of its own blockade of Iranian ports and associated vessels.
Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, a central figure in the country's efforts to mediate between Iran and the U.S., was expected to return for a new visit to Tehran on Tuesday, but Iran played down any hope for new wider peace talks.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said talks with Munir "relate to issues concerning the negotiations, but they are mainly focused on bilateral relations and strengthening interactions and cooperation."

Surprise! Hot on the heels of PlayStation's own upscaling tech announcements, Microsoft and AMD just revealed that the firm's flagship FSR 4.1 tech is coming to the Xbox platform.
FSR (FidelityFX Super Resolution) is a technology from AMD that renders games at a lower resolution, and then uses machine learning to generate a sharper image. Since the hardware isn't working as hard, that overhead can be used for performance.
FSR 4.1 is a big leap over previous versions, and Microsoft has partnered with AMD to bring it not only to Xbox Series X , but also Xbox Ally X and Xbox Series S — the latter of which should benefit from very, very big performance boosts as a result.
"At Xbox, we're building a gaming platform designed to meet players where they are, and make it easier for creators to reach them," Xbox CTO Scott Van Vilet explained. "AMD has been an important partner in that journey for more than two decades. Together our teams have been pushing gaming forward, across Xbox and Windows. From the silicon at the heart of our consoles and handhelds, to technologies like DirectX, Advanced Shader Delivery, and AutoSR that helps developers get more from the hardware and deliver better experiences for our players."
"Today, we're excited to take another step forward together. With FSR 4.1 coming to Xbox. Now, we've worked very closely with AMD to optimize this technology, giving developers another powerful tool for great performance and visual quality for players. Now, whether you're playing on an Xbox Ally handheld, as well as coming soon to Xbox Series X and Series S consoles. And this is just the beginning. Our teams are continuing to work together across hardware and software, and there's even more ahead with Project Helix, leveraging FSR Diamond to power what comes next."
It's unclear exactly when these technologies will roll out to Xbox devices. It sounds as though FSR 4.1 will hit Xbox Ally X before the year end, but Xbox Series X|S are listed as "coming soon," with no exact window offered.
Sadly, it seems the Xbox Ally base model is fully incompatible with FSR 4.1, which is a bit of a shame, but it should prove transformative for those with the Xbox Ally X and the just-released Xbox Ally X20 , as well as the Xbox Series S.
The Xbox Series S has historically been difficult for developers owing to its irregular RAM allocation, but if FSR 4.1 can do some of the heavy lifting, it should ease the pressure on developers to deliver a native 1080p image.
We're reaching out to Microsoft for some clarification on timelines and will get back to you if we hear from them.

Jez is known for breaking exclusive news and analysis as relates to the Microsoft ecosystem — while being powered by tea. articles.title_orig: Hegseth Said to Make Unannounced Visit to Israel for Talks With Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Hegseth Said to Make Unannounced Visit to Israel for Talks With Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, three Israeli officials said, as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran .
Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the prime minister, later confirmed to Reuters that Netanyahu had met with Hegseth at the Uvda Air Force Base in Israel’s southern Negev desert region.
Netanyahu and Hegseth discussed “the threats in the region” and the U.S.-Israel partnership in dealing both offensively and defensively with those threats, he said in a brief phone call.
Hegseth also thanked Israel for hosting U.S. forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed President Donald Trump’s support for the prime minister.
“There’s a deep personal relationship here that was at the core of this discussion,” Spielman said.
On Sunday, Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election in Israel, the country’s first ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel.
The Pentagon has not publicly commented on Hegseth’s visit.
Hegseth earlier posted on X that he had visited U.S. service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.
He did not specify where he had met with the forces.
Hegseth’s visit comes as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz and as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.
U.S. and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off the wider Middle East war. Netanyahu told Israeli media this month that he’s not seeking to attack Iran before the Oct. 27 Israeli election. Trump has said he will not attack Iran before U.S. midterm elections in November.
Israel has hosted additional U.S. forces, including military aircraft, since at least February as part of the war with Iran.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street gains as healthcare stocks rally, oil prices fall
articles.title_zh: Wall Street gains as healthcare stocks rally, oil prices fall
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose on Tuesday as a number of upbeat earnings reports and a drop in oil prices overshadowed recent pressure seen among artificial intelligence-related stocks.
The blue-chip index gained 504 points, or 1%, while the S&P 500 added 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite traded up 0.2%.
Shares of industrial and safety products producer 3M offered a boost to the Dow, jumping more than 5% following better-than-expected earnings results and a full-year guidance raise . Shares of aerospace and defense company Northrop Grumman also advanced more than 5% after it posted an earnings beat.
Meanwhile, oil prices pulled back from earlier gains, helping investor sentiment. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were last down less than 1% at around $103 per barrel, while Brent crude futures fell about 1% to roughly $108 a barrel. The moves in oil, which added to the declines in Treasury yields , come as traders continued to monitor developments in the Middle East.
The market has been weighed down as of late by worries about the sustainability of the AI trade amid debt and demand concerns. In fact, sentiment in tech took a hit earlier in the day after Korean AI firm Elice tumbled more than 30% overnight in its public market debut. Asia-Pacific markets declined Tuesday, after U.S. stocks rose overnight, leading to declines in the South Korean market.
However, AI-related stocks staged a bit of a comeback as the session went on. Micron Technology , Sandisk and Advanced Micro Devices all rose around 1%. Intel climbed more than 1%, while Seagate Technology , was up more than 2%. CoreWeave gained more than 2%.
The S&P 500 finished in positive territory on Monday, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced more than 1%. That marked a rebound from last week's rout, when anxieties around companies borrowing too much money for their AI build-outs intensified.
"For much of this year, the market has been willing to look through higher rates because the growth story, notably that around AI, was strong enough to justify it. Last week, we saw that relationship begin to be tested," said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion.
"Hyperscalers report over the next few weeks, setting up the next major stress test for the AI trade," he continued. "Guidance around ROI, data center spending and 2027 capex will arguably be more important than the headline earnings figures."

TD Cowen upgraded BlackRock to buy from hold on Tuesday, citing the company is ahead of revenue and operating income targets.
TD Cowen's Bill Katz also increased the company's price target to $1,405, a nearly 25% upside from Monday's close.
Katz added that BlackRock has several avenues for organic growth, including in private markets and retirement.
3M shares popped more than 5% after the producer of industrial and safety products posted adjusted earnings of $2.50 per share, more than the LSEG estimate of $2.38 per share.
Shares of GE Aerospace were off 2% after the company reported its third-quarter financials, where the company delivered an earnings and revenue beat.
GE Aerospace reported adjusted earnings of $2.25 per share, compared to analysts polled by LSEG's estimates for $2.01 per share. Revenue also came in above expectations at $13.29 billion.
The company also hiked guidance across various metrics for the full-year, however free cash flow at $2.04 billion was lower than expectations for $2.2 billion, according to StreetAccount.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began Tuesday's session in the red.
The broad market index fell 0.2% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq pulled back 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline.
Investor concerns over CoreWeave 's credit ticked higher on Tuesday, with the spread on its five-year credit default swap rising back up near levels seen on Thursday .
The CDS, which is a way for buyers to pay for protection in case the borrower defaults, last saw spreads over 1,121, which is up 2.22% for the day and more than 17% over the past week. Spreads of 1,000 or greater are generally considered a sign of distress.
Housing starts slumped in September, raising fresh concerns about the state of the real estate market as the Federal Reserve contemplates additional interest rate hikes.
The Commerce Department reported Tuesday that privately owned starts totaled 1.22 million at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. That was off 5.2% from the August level and well below the Dow Jones consensus for 1.3 million.
Additionally, single-family starts weakened, totaling 859,000, off 4.6% from the prior month.
Building permits issued during the month were slightly better than expected, totaling a seasonally adjusted annualized 1.4 million, against the estimate for 1.39 million. The total was 0.2% below August.

General Motors beat Wall Street's expectations on the top- and bottom-lines as it reported its Q3 2026 earnings, delivering strong results driven by high truck sales and growing subscription revenue
The company raised its free cash flow expectations and narrowed its 2026 full-year guidance.
The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion, but didn't provide a specific timeframe for the repurchase.
"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.
GM expects commodity inflation costs to be nearly $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed."
GM stock was off roughly 7% during premarket trading despite the beats.
Korean AI firm Elice tumbled more than 30% overnight in its public market debut. Investors recently have been worried about the sustainability of the AI trade, as debt and demand concerns grow .
Shares of Solstice Advanced Materials , which was spun off from Honeywell last year, rose more than 3% after The Financial Times reported, citing sources, that activist Starboard Value had built a stake in the company.
Starboard wants Solstice to cut about $100 million in corporate costs focus on its refrigerants and nuclear businesses, the report said . Solstice shares are up more than 24% year to date.
Northrop Grumman gained more than 1% after the defense contractor reported mixed results for the third quarter.
The company earned $7.89 per barrel, beating an LSEG estimate of $7.18 per share. However, revenue of $11.12 billion was just below the $11.14 billion consensus.
ABB CEO Morten Wierod told CNBC he sees no slowdown in the AI data center buildout in the coming years, despite investors becoming wary of ballooning AI spend .
The Swiss multinational firm declined around 6% on Tuesday, even after reporting record third-quarter orders , which jumped 40% to $12 billion, driven by a triple-digit increase in its data center segment.
"ABB without data centers, it is a double-digit growth when you look at the order intake," Wierod told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe."
"I believe there is a strong trend...you will see a continued build-out of the data center capacity in the coming years," Wierod added.
Other data center stocks were also down Tuesday. Schneider Electric and Siemens Energy fell 3% and 4%, respectively. Meanwhile, neocloud companies Coreweave and Nebius were both down around 3% in premarket trading.
Asia-Pacific markets closed in the red on Tuesday, with South Korean equities leading the losses.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.content_orig:
U.S. envoys were meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.
President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war . Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”
Witkoff had been set to meet with Zelenskyy in Oslo, with Kushner joining via videoconference, the Norwegian government said earlier. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb was also joining the talks, it added.
Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.
Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the Midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.
In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.
“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.
Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”
Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.
When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”
Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.
“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.
Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“ The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

A Massachusetts-based manufacturer has recalled more than 1.5 million pounds of various meat products over serious potential health concerns.
Kayem Foods Inc. initiated the recall after learning that the items may not have been stored at the correct temperature. It has since been deemed a Class I recall by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service, meaning “there is a reasonable probability that the use of the product will cause serious, adverse health consequences or death.”
An investigation that began after a customer reported receiving a warm product delivery on October 1 revealed that a warehouse cooler experienced temperature fluctuations while storing the items, according to FSIS.
Approximately 1,584,361 recalled items were manufactured between March 31, 2026 and October 7, 2026 and are labeled with the establishment numbers “EST. M/P 7839,” “EST. P 20935A” or “EST. M 9520” inside the USDA inspection mark. Affected items were shipped to retail and food service locations across the U.S. and Hong Kong.
Products include various brands of hot dogs, bacon, sausage, and deli meat. A full list of affected items can be found here .
There have been no reports of illness, but customers in possession of recalled products should discard them or return them to the place of purchase.
The meat recall comes amid a slew of issues affecting consumers.
Over 112,000 bottles of pain relievers sold by Amazon were voluntarily recalled last week due to discoloration. The news was shared in an enforcement report from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration .
Various bottles of 500-milligram Extra Strength Acetaminophen caplets sold across the U.S. have been affected. Customer complaints about discolored tablets led to the voluntary recall initiated by Amazon, according to the report.
Included in the recall are 90,456 500-count bottles, 14,640 200-count bottles, and 7,836 1000-count bottles, all with various lot numbers and expiration dates between September 30, 2027 and February 29, 2028.
No injuries or adverse health effects related to the discoloration of the tablets have been reported.
Amazon has contacted customers who have purchased affected bottles for refund information. Customers can check their order history and product lot numbers on Amazon’s website .
A pre-workout powder has also been recalled after it was found to contain an illegal and dangerous stimulant , the FDA said last week.
A batch of “Leader Formulas, LLC RAPTURE Preworkout” sold online and in stores between January 2025 and May 2026 was made with “1,3-Dimethylamylamine,” also known as “ DMAA .”
DMAA is a synthetic chemical developed from amphetamine, sometimes used in dietary supplements that can spike blood pressure and lead to heart attacks, shortness of breath and tightening of the chest.

“I’m embarrassed on a world stage,” said a regretful Trump voter in a Navigator Research focus group shared first with The 19th.
Two years ago, six White suburban mothers were among the more than 77 million Americans who voted to put President Donald Trump back in the White House. Now, they say they regret it.
In a recent focus group convened by Navigator Research, a Democratic polling and public opinion firm, and shared exclusively with The 19th, the six Trump voters discussed their disappointment with his second term — and their mixed feelings about the upcoming midterm elections. Navigator shared the group with The 19th on the condition that the participants be referred to only by their first names to protect their privacy.
Chrissy, a 44-year-old woman from Michigan, said that two years ago, she was “lazy” in basing her vote on political ads and discussions with others instead of her own research.
The 19th thanks our sponsors. Become one .
Now, she’s committed to voting for candidates who will check Trump.
“He’s pushed the country into an authoritarian playbook,” she said. “And if we don’t do something to stop it right now, it’s unlikely that there’ll be much left.”
Trump is also losing women who were once among his most committed backers.
“I was a die-hard supporter, but it’s been a complete backstab since, pretty much, the storming of the Capitol for me,” said Kristen, a 39-year-old woman in Ohio. “That’s when my opinion really started changing about how he is as a leader.”
Nicole, a 47-year-old in Texas, could relate. She believes Trump “might have his intentions in the right place,” but his second term hasn’t matched his campaign promises. She knows people struggling to afford groceries and turning to public assistance programs to make ends meet, and she thinks things “will get worse before they get better.”
“I just feel we’re drowning, and it only started when Trump got in office,” she said. “I was fully, like she said, a die-hard fan of Trump. I mean, flag supporter, everything. Now I feel like I regret voting for him, I’ll just be honest.”
Melissa Toufanian, a managing director at Navigator, said their research has found that 1 in 4 people who voted for Trump in 2024 now regret it. Moms are more likely to regret their votes than dads — and suburban women are a critical election demographic for both parties.
While all the focus group participants have soured on Trump, they aren’t all sold on Democrats. Several expressed deep disillusionment with politics and doubted their votes could meaningfully change what they see as a broken status quo upheld by both political parties.
“I do think in a lot of ways that our voice doesn’t matter anymore,” said Gayle, a 47-year-old in Florida. “I think Congress sucks, honestly. I just think it sucks. I don’t think that they’re in it for the people. I think they’re in it for themselves these days, and it’s really on both sides.”
The cost of living consistently ranks as voters’ top concern, and many Democratic candidates are putting affordability front and center in their campaigns. Polling from The 19th and YouGov found that women are more worried than men about paying for groceries, healthcare, housing and retirement.
Even women who weren’t as personally affected by rising prices saw the war in Iran and the resulting increase in gas and fuel prices as a clear about-face from Trump’s 2024 campaign promises to lower costs.
“I’m not struggling, but so many people are,” said Denise, a 49-year-old woman from Ohio. “I’m repulsed about the tariffs that we’ve put on our neighbor in Canada, the war, basically picking on other countries and just starting a war for no reason.”
Of the entire group, Gayle had the most positive assessment of Trump’s second term and the economy. But she said she regretted voting for him because of the war in Iran, which “really messed things up.”
“If you’re looking at the gas prices versus if I’m going to see a nuclear bomb happen, I’m more concerned with my gas prices than I am with the nuclear bomb, to be honest,” she said.
And it wasn’t just the economy that made the women in the focus group turn against Trump.
Denise pointed to Trump “taking down history because he’s a narcissist” in tearing down the East Wing of the White House to build a new ballroom.
“It just … that disgusts me,” she said. “He had no right to do that, and that’s one of the big things that pissed me off.”
Women in the focus group said that while they supported enforcing immigration laws and securing the border, they thought the government had gone too far.
“I’m not against the deportation, I’m against inhumane treatment in that process,” said Kristen, the 39-year-old in Ohio.
Brandy, a 43-year-old woman in North Carolina, said she was particularly troubled by federal immigration officials killing two U.S. citizens , Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minnesota. She said when she posted about Good’s killing on Facebook, she was attacked by her friends who are “extreme Trump lovers.”
“He just makes people lose their human decency,” she said.
And they didn’t view other members of the Trump administration much more favorably. They used words like “terrible,” “compromised,” “Trump’s twin,” and “corrupt” to describe Vice President JD Vance. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was called “a liar,” and Robert F. Kennedy Jr.  “uneducated.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth “should have stayed on TV,” Kristen said.
But despite the group’s collective distaste for Trump and his inner circle, not all plan to vote for Democrats down the ballot in November.
Denise in Ohio said she was leaning toward voting for Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio’s race for governor over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, whom she described as “up [Trump’s] rear end,” while Gayle in Florida said she planned to vote for the Republican, Rep. Byron Donalds, in her state’s gubernatorial race.
Brandy said she didn’t like former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in North Carolina, but was voting for him because of GOP nominee Michael Whatley’s ties to a convicted sex offender who served in several leadership positions in the state Republican Party, something Democratic groups have spent millions highlighting in campaign ads.
“I’m gonna go for the guy that doesn’t have a buddy that’s a sex offender,” she said. “Even though I don’t like him, he is the lesser of two evils.”
Toufanian said Democrats have a big opportunity to focus on issues suburban women care about “and to really make some tangible improvements in their lives.”
Food quality and safety is one of those issues. Nearly all the women cited it as a top concern, but only two had heard of the acronym MAHA, or Make America Healthy Again .
“I think there’s a real opportunity because it touches on so many of the other issues that are so important in this election cycle, particularly corruption and affordability,” Toufanian said.
Most women in the focus group said they’re taking a wait-and-see approach to the 2028 presidential race. Two, Chrissy and Kristen, said they were open to voting for a Democrat but wouldn’t want to vote for Vance or former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee.
Chrissy said she’d primarily evaluate Republican candidates on whether they would further the “cruelty” and “highly polarized” atmosphere cultivated by Trump.

articles.title_orig: Apple explains why HomeView couldn’t launch until now
articles.title_zh: Apple explains why HomeView couldn’t launch until now
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s new HomeView was reportedly mostly finished for years, but kept getting delayed. Here’s why HomeView couldn’t launch until now, per quotes from key Apple execs.
In November 2024, Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on the product we now know as HomeView. At the time, he said Apple was targeting a March 2025 launch. But that date kept slipping, and now HomeView will finally arrive in homes on November 13, 2026.
Why the long wait? Gurman has repeatedly pointed to Siri AI as the chief cause of delays. And Apple execs have now largely confirmed that in quotes given to The Verge .
Jennifer Pattison Tuohy asked Kaiann Drance, Apple’s VP of product marketing for home, why now was the right time for HomeView and Apple’s renewed smart home push.
She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.
HomeView is being marketed as a shared device that taps into users’ personal context in a way that wasn’t possible pre-Siri AI. So it’s easy to see how Apple’s main pitch would need to change without the more personalized Siri.
A similar explanation was given by Apple’s Lilian Rincon, VP of product marketing for AI. She told The Verge that Siri AI is core to HomeView because it’s “much more capable” and also highlighted its conversational abilities, which make it easy to use for any family member.
“It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”
This emphasis and explanation also makes HomeView’s absence in the EU more understandable.
If Siri AI was simply a nice-to-have addition to an otherwise feature-rich product, perhaps it could launch in the EU still. But if the whole value proposition revolves around the new assistant and its personalized features, waiting until Siri AI is available for iOS in the EU makes more sense.
You can read The Verge’s full article here for more quotes and context.
What do you think of Apple’s explanation for the HomeView’s launch timing? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq mixed as AI trade rebound stalls
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq mixed as AI trade rebound stalls
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks climbed on Tuesday as chip stocks trimmed losses and investors turned their focus to a slew of earnings out this week.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.9%, and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) erased its decline, climbing 0.2% after the major averages closed mixed on Monday, as tech stocks rebounded.
The AI trade came into focus on Tuesday after Elice ( 0158S0.KQ ), a South Korean data center provider, saw its shares plunge 32% during its public debut in Seoul, underscoring lingering concerns about the health of the AI trade.
Investors turned their attention to a fresh round of corporate earnings this week. General Motors ( GM ) tightened its profit outlook but announced a $20 billion share buyback program . United Airlines ( UAL ) will report after the close.
Streaming giant Netflix ( NFLX ) will report quarterly earnings after the bell on Tuesday. EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ) and social media giant Meta ( META ) are expected to post results on Wednesday.
On the economic front, housing starts fell to a four-month low amid soft demand, with mortgage rates remaining elevated.
Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ) fell to $108 per barrel while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) traded below $98.
Qualcomm ( QCOM ) shares rose 1% following a report that the designer of chips for smartphones plans to start cutting jobs globally next month as part of a "performance-focused reduction" following employee reviews.
The plan was outlined in a memo to staff from CEO Cristiano Amon, which Reuters reviewed. Notifications are set to start in November.
The memo did not specify how many positions would be affected.
Qualcomm shares are up more than 2% year-to-date.
Wall Street is in a buying mood. The AI trade's leaders had to bleed a little before joining in.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) slipped below Friday's close early, giving back Monday's rebound from an eight-session losing streak, as my colleague Ines Ferré reported . Then buyers showed up right at the summer floor near 11,000.
Chart watchers know this setup.
A dip below support that quickly reverses is a bear trap , catching traders who bet on a breakdown. But it only counts if chips close back above Friday's level.
And history says don't relax yet. After every losing streak of seven sessions or more since 1994, the index traded below the streak's final close within a month. After the longest ones, it was lower a month later most of the time.
A BofA Global Research report calls last week's rout a "positioning-driven hiccup on the fringes of the AI trade." The credit market isn't so sure. The cost of insuring Oracle's debt is at its highest since at least 2021, and even the megacaps' default swaps are creeping up.
A close above 11,137 springs the trap. Lose 11,000, and the next stop is closer to 10,450.
US stocks were mixed at Tuesday's open as investors weighed another batch of corporate earnings against pressure from higher government bond yields.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.4% while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 0.1%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) declined 0.5% after the major averages closed mixed on Monday as tech stocks rebounded.
Investors remain focused on whether strong third-quarter earnings can keep stocks moving higher after last week's volatility. At Tuesday's open the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) hovered at 5.10%, keeping pressure on stock valuations though easing over the last week.
AI infrastructure stocks are under pressure again before the opening bell. CoreWeave ( CRWV ) is taking the hardest hit.
The AI cloud provider is trading at its lowest level since May 2025 premarket, extending a slide of more than 40% since Oct. 6.
So what's spooking investors? The debt. CoreWeave borrowed heavily to build its data centers, and its bonds sold off across maturities last week, as my colleague Brian Sozzi reported .
Siebert Financial chief investment officer Mark Malek isn't rushing in. Some AI stocks are "honestly down for the right reason," he said Monday on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. He "wouldn't back up the truck."
Every chip stock trading premarket in a 60-stock Yahoo Finance semiconductor basket is lower, with SK hynix ( SKHY ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) among the hardest hit. The rest of the market is calmer, with S&P 500 gainers outnumbering decliners roughly 3 to 2.
Monday's low of $59.25 is the line in the sand. A snap back above it would make this breakdown a bear trap — a fake-out that burns traders betting on more losses.
Stay below, and the next stops are around $53, then the all-time low at $33 and change.
Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
GM ( GM ) posted third quarter results before the bell that topped estimates. The automaker tightened its full-year profit outlook instead of boosting it, but issued shareholders a new $20 billion share repurchase program instead.
For the quarter, GM posted Q3 revenue of $50.0 billion, up 2.9% from a year ago and above the $48.52 billion Bloomberg consensus. GM posted adjusted EPS of $3.70 vs $3.57 estimated, with adjusted EBIT coming in at $4.1 billion, ahead of the $4.02 billion expected and up nearly 22%.
President Trump announced an $8 billion aid package on Monday to help US farmers pay for diesel this harvest season.
The relief program, announced at a campaign rally in Kansas and on social media, aims to bring down fuel costs for Americans ahead of next month's midterm elections.
"Tonight, I am also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new 'Harvest Fuel Relief Program,' providing our Farmers with 8 BILLION DOLLARS in support to offset Diesel costs during this Harvest Season," Trump's account posted on Truth Social ( DJT ).

articles.title_orig: SpaceX earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: SpaceX earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX ( SPCX ) will report highly anticipated third quarter results on Tuesday after the bell, only its second report as a public company. The report comes as the stock has recovered in recent weeks.
After shedding nearly 30% after its $150 market debut in its first few weeks as a public company, SpaceX stock recovered in Q3 and is now trading around its debut price.
As for the quarter itself, SpaceX is expected to report Q3 revenue of $12.7 billion per Bloomberg consensus, up sequentially from the $7.8 billion in Q2. SpaceX is expected to post adjusted EPS of $0.15, with adjusted EBITDA of $6.59 billion.
Key to SpaceX's quarterly results is what happens in its AI unit, now called SpaceXSI. Last quarter, the unit posted an operating loss of $1.26 billion versus estimates of $2.39 billion, with AI spending ballooning to $15.8 billion in the quarter, larger than expected and much higher than the $7.7 billion spent in Q1.
The concern is that this AI spending keeps ballooning as SpaceX continues investing in data centers like Colossus and AI products like Grok and its agent, Grok Bot, and whether the company can secure the financing it needs to sustain infrastructure spending.
"Need for additional financing remains a key overhang for sentiment, especially given the recent neocloud debt saga," Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas wrote in a note published on Monday. "This is the biggest risk to our model, and we do not want to downplay it — although a hypothetical world where SpaceX cannot raise financing likely has much broader implications for the economy and the rest of an investor's portfolio." Read more .
While Wall Street was still in a state of disbelief late last week that Elon Musk made a flying Tesla ( TSLA ) Roadster, his SpaceX ( SPCX ) team came out with a not-so-small note on its investor relations page.
SpaceX earnings are coming out on Oct. 20 after the market close. The announcement was a surprise to many on the Street, as it's common practice for earnings release dates to be shared weeks in advance.
But there may be a few reasons behind SpaceX's rushed earnings date.
"Possible explanations include a desire to put updated financials on record ahead of further financing arrangements or share time-sensitive operational/strategic updates — either before counterparties do or to give the market time to digest the implications ahead of the sizeable lock-up releases (1.30 billion shares two days after earnings, 329 million on 10/24, and the remaining 857 million tranche of the 180-day group thereafter). Or the explanation could be as mundane as scheduling — it's just hard to know," said Evercore ISI analyst Kutgun Maral.
The deciding factor on if SpaceX ( SPCX ) shares truly l ift-off in 2027 may revolve around what's happening down on Mother Earth, specifically on how much computing power the company is selling to a hungry world of AI infrastructure builders.
"Looking forward to next year, the largest swing factor in respect to forecasts will be compute deployment, in our view. Management is targeting >2 GW exiting 4Q26, which we think is doable, and then 5-10 GW exiting 2027. We continue to model toward the low end at ~6 GW and have line of sight into procuring 5-7 GW of power over the next couple of years," says Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu.
A combined SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) would haul in some serious coin, Cathie Wood's Ark Invest said in a new note.
The Elon Musk bull's firm estimated that SpaceX and Tesla could generate $3.8 trillion in sales and $2.7 trillion in operating profits by 2031, with SpaceX contributing roughly 62% and 69%, respectively.
To get a sense of how bullish a call this is, Yahoo Finance data shows that Wall Street analysts expect SpaceX to post $43 billion in sales this year, while Tesla clocks in at $107 billion.
"While our model assesses Tesla as a standalone business, a SpaceX-Tesla merger could take place within the next five years," the Ark Invest team said. "Tesla's highly cash-generative robotaxi network could help fund SpaceX's ambitious plans for orbital data centers, and at the same time SpaceX's compute-intensive frontier AI models could serve as the planning layer for Optimus deployments. Working together on the Terafab project, both companies could alleviate chip constraints."

articles.title_orig: Australian MP hit by vehicle has leg amputated - as suspect's father says she is family friend
articles.title_zh: Australian MP hit by vehicle has leg amputated - as suspect's father says she is family friend
articles.content_orig:
A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday.
The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.
Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime".
Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs.
"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.
"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."
They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".
Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.
Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.
She was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help.
A local barber who was there says he pulled the suspect out of his car.
"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way," said Ricky Jefferies.
Others who helped "didn't even check for danger", he added. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."
In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.
As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarrawingee, around 12km (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta.
"At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.
Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.
The community, and country, remain in shock.
At a vigil on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the aisle of the Holy Trinity Cathedral, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who came to pay their respects.
Wangaratta's main street, where Haines's office is located, had reopened to traffic. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.
One card read: "May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world."

articles.title_orig: Oil prices move higher as traders adjust to a new normal in the Middle East
articles.title_zh: Oil prices move higher as traders adjust to a new normal in the Middle East
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices surged in early trading Tuesday, as energy markets adjusted to a new normal in the Middle East. The increase in crude prices threatened to drive up the cost of gas in the United States just two weeks before the midterm elections.
U.S. crude prices jumped as much as 5% to about $109 a barrel, the highest price since April, while the price of international Brent crude climbed 1.5% to more than $111, its highest price since May. Prices pulled back later in the morning, after weaker-than-expected U.S. housing starts raised the prospect of a broader slowdown and lower demand.
Prices for advanced oil contracts dated for next year also hit record highs , “implying an extended period of high oil prices deep into 2027,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note Tuesday.
“The 2027 contracts are moving higher as well as the possible reality of higher for longer oil prices sink in,” Peter Boockvar, author of the Boock Report and chief investment officer of OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners, said in a note Tuesday.
High gas prices have become a major issue for voters in the midterms, where Republicans face dwindling odds of maintaining their control of Congress.
A recent NBC News poll found that 67% of U.S. adults believe gas prices are a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. A majority also said that current economic conditions have caused them to change their spending habits.
U.S. gasoline prices had started off the week lower. At $4.28 a gallon, the national average price of unleaded was on pace to reach its lowest level in a month.
But that trend is likely to be upended as higher crude prices filter through to the pump.
Several factors were contributing to Tuesday’s oil price hikes.
The cost of chartering a large tanker vessel to transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz has quadrupled since September, data shows.
Much of that increase is a risk premium, both for sailors and insurance. During the past two weeks, at least 18 ⁠vessels have been attacked in the strait, the ship-tracking group Kpler said in a note ⁠Monday.
The higher cost of transport has begun to offset the recent bump in supply from a growing number of ships moving through the strait.
The Iranian attacks on ships have also prompted investor speculation that the Trump administration will be more likely to escalate against Iran after the midterms, the Deutsche Bank analysts said.
Iran-aligned Houthi rebels also claimed Monday that they had hit airport, energy and military targets in Saudi Arabia, as well as a ​training camp in Yemen for that government’s security forces.
The U.K. will begin deploying fighter jets over Saudi Arabia to help protect against further Houthi attacks, the Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The entry of another country’s military into the regional hostilities was taken as a further sign of escalating tensions.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Curfews bring calm to Paris as France cracks down on weekend rioters
articles.title_zh: Curfews bring calm to Paris as France cracks down on weekend rioters
articles.content_orig:
France is on fire, and it faces a political and an economic reckoning that feels dangerously familiar to Americans.
The country is nearing a fiscal crisis, because it spent more than it can afford to pay back. The bill is coming due much faster than expected after bond rates surged in recent months, boosted by rising energy costs. Raising taxes and reducing government spending are part of a potential solution, but those would be politically unpopular decisions that could risk further angering an already livid public . Any workable solution faces a steep climb in an uncertain budget battle in a sharply divided government.
A growing number of countries are facing struggles similar to France’s — in particular, the United Kingdom — where rapidly growing debt, surging costs to finance that borrowing and insufficient political will to make the uncomfortable decisions to solve the problem are the story of Western economics right now. That includes the United States.
But similarities can be superficial.
France’s financial stress is particularly acute. The risk of contagion throughout Europe is low. France’s enormous public safety net represents a much larger share of government spending than that in the United States. And the unique dynamics of the American economy means the United States faces no imminent danger of becoming the next France.
These are not new problems: Europe’s social safety net has been on an unsustainable path for decades, and economists and some politicians have warned for years that the bill would eventually come due.
But they’re getting worse. The Iran war exacerbated the West’s fiscal problems.
Since February, the G7 economies’ average 10-year government bond yield grew more than 1 percentage point, reaching the highest level in nearly 20 years, the International Monetary Fund reported last week.
By the end of the decade, those seven economies’ public debt loads are expected to collectively exceed their economic production, the IMF predicts. That would be the first time since World War II.
France’s public debt is around 119% of its GDP, double the European Union’s target, and its annual budget deficit is 5.4% of its gross domestic product.
“In Europe, people are increasingly scared of the bond market and the interest rates that governments need to pay to borrow,” said Peter Taylor-Gooby, a social policy professor at the University of Kent. “It’s come to a point where you can’t ignore it anymore. If we do, we’ll reach a serious crisis.”
The rioting across France is a symptom of a much larger public and political crisis
On paper, America doesn’t look dissimilar: Its $32 trillion public debt is roughly equal to annual US GDP, and the $2 trillion budget deficit that it just closed the books on is more than 6% of GDP. The cost to finance America’s public debt just crossed $1 trillion a year , an astounding 14% of the total federal budget.
In other words, one in every seven tax dollars is used just to pay interest on the amount of money the United States is borrowing.
But the serious conversations about cutting back on spending and raising taxes taking place in Europe are considerably less serious in the United States. So why isn’t the United States facing the same problems as France?
The United States’ biggest advantage is that it prints the world’s reserve currency. The majority of global transactions are conducted in US dollars, including key commodities like oil and gold.
Demand for dollars remains robust in large part because they’re considered safe: The United States’ transparency and commitment to the rule of law make the dollar the cornerstone of the global financial system — even if some of the shine has worn off over the past decade.
That also fuels demand for US Treasuries, widely considered the safest of safe-haven assets. Even in the midst of a global government bond sell-off, US bond rates remain lower than those of other Western economies. And when stocks went on a skid last week, investors were unafraid to turn to their traditional place of refuge, sending Treasury yields sharply lower in the process.
But the difference between France and the United States really comes down to one thing. As James Carville said: It’s the economy, stupid.
The United States also has a uniquely large and diverse economy that is far less susceptible to shocks than many of its smaller peers. AI in particular is producing an investment boom in the United States that is lifting the economy when several other sectors appear to be stagnating or in decline.
One key way to make deficits less relevant is to keep the economy growing strong. That makes the debt look puny by comparison.
So countries need to ask: What is the rate we’re paying — and is it sustainable for us to keep paying it based on our expected economic growth?”
“France and the UK are pretty close,” noted Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “But in the US, AI’s contributions to growth make it more likely we’ll manage our debts and navigate it much more gracefully.”
Economists warn: Don’t confuse the lack of a looming debt crisis in the United States with fiscal responsibility. It’s just that it can handle the problem better than France or the UK.
“That doesn’t mean we should take any solace in that,” added Zandi. “We’re just in a different place.”
Any time a European country faces a fiscal problem, it raises concerns about a contagion that could spread across the continent. But economists widely view France’s problems as contained within the country.
The European Central Bank has signaled it would not need to intervene in France’s fiscal situation. But it could if it had to, and it is well-positioned to buy up a bunch of bonds of its member countries to limit any potential contagion effects, noted Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.
Other European economies’ deficits are also much smaller by comparison. Some are expected to run surpluses this year.
And French political parties across the left and right have said they want to remain with the European Union — including French presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, a far-right candidate who once championed “Frexit” but has since backed off that pledge. Although Germany’s AfD party has advocated leaving the EU, it isn’t close to forming a government yet, Kenningham noted.
But an X factor could lead to a debt crisis outside France: the US “X date.” At some point next year, the United States will hit its debt ceiling again, and the new Congress will need to negotiate with President Donald Trump to raise it — a political football that could be particularly challenged by a lame duck president and a potentially Democratic-controlled Congress less willing to give in.
A failure to raise the debt ceiling threatens to force the United States to manufacture a default on its debt, even if it otherwise would be able to pay.
“You could construct a scenario in which we breach the debt limit by Halloween next year,” said Zandi. “And then you’ve got other issues.”

articles.title_orig: Walmart rolls out new bundle combining Walmart+, Sam’s Club Plus
articles.title_zh: Walmart rolls out new bundle combining Walmart+, Sam’s Club Plus
articles.content_orig:
LSEG head of consumer research Jharonne Marti discusses the mind of the consumer and the Walmart overreaction on 'Making Money.'
Walmart announced Tuesday it is rolling out a new membership bundle that gives shoppers access to both Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus for $120 a year, nearly $100 less than purchasing the two memberships separately.
The bundle works out to the equivalent of $10 per month, though Walmart said it will only be available as an annual membership and will not include a monthly option or free trial.
Walmart CEO John Furner told FOX Business that the retail giant wanted to roll out the combined membership ahead of the holiday season, when many households are looking for ways to save both money and time.
"It does help at a time when we do see some customers showing some signs of pressure," Furner said, pointing in particular to higher energy costs.
SAM’S CLUB EXPANDS THANKSGIVING MEAL, KEEPING COST UNDER $10 A PERSON AS INFLATION WEIGHS ON CONSUMERS
Walmart said the combined membership costs almost $100 less annually than paying for Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus separately. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The launch comes after Walmart reported continued growth across its membership and e-commerce businesses in its most recent quarterly results in August.
During the company's second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call on Aug. 20, Furner said membership fee revenue increased 17% to an all-time high.
"Marketplace, fulfillment services, membership, advertising and other commerce solutions are strengthening our business, and they are improving the economics of the company," he said at the time.
WALMART DOUBLES DOWN ON PLEDGE AGAINST AI-POWERED PERSONALIZED PRICING
Furner also said Walmart+ membership grew by double digits during the quarter, while Sam's Club membership posted growth in the U.S., China and Mexico.
He told FOX Business that the bundle is designed to appeal across income levels.
WALMART EXPANDS DRONE DELIVERY TO 2 MAJOR US CITIES
Walmart+ currently costs $98 for the standard annual plan, while Sam's Club Plus costs $120 a year.
The new bundle rivals Amazon Prime, which costs $139 annually.
Members will receive the benefits of both programs, including free delivery from Walmart and Sam’s Club, access to Sam’s Club locations and member-only pricing, a choice between Peacock and Paramount+, gas discounts and 2% Sam’s Cash on eligible purchases, according to the retailer.
Furner said Walmart aims to have the bundle encourage existing Walmart+ members to shop at Sam’s Club and also appeal to consumers who currently have memberships elsewhere.
"We're deciding to do this from a position of strength and momentum," Furner said.
Annual Walmart+ members can add Sam’s Club Plus for an additional $22 per year, while existing Sam’s Club members can upgrade to Plus for $60 and receive Walmart+ at no additional cost.
Current Sam’s Club Plus members will be able to activate Walmart+ at no additional charge.
Inflation accelerated in September, with higher energy costs helping push consumer prices higher. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Walmart also said U.S. field associates at Walmart and Sam’s Club will receive access to both memberships as part of their employee benefits.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The new offering comes as consumers continue to contend with higher prices. Inflation climbed 3.7% in September from a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index. Gasoline prices rose more than 34% over the past year, while grocery prices climbed 1.8%.

articles.title_orig: Review: Stupid Never Dies (PS5) - Toilet-Flushing, Monster-Munching Roguelite Stands Out in a Stacked Genre
articles.title_zh: Review: Stupid Never Dies (PS5) - Toilet-Flushing, Monster-Munching Roguelite Stands Out in a Stacked Genre
articles.content_orig:
With a scribblecore aesthetic and a story so unhinged it’d make even Suda51 smile, Stupid Never Dies is not your average roguelite.
I think that’s important, because this debut action effort from Japanese dev GPTRACK50 is entering a genre that’s quickly becoming overstuffed with options.
Davy’s descent into the inner-sanctums of the earth’s demonic core doesn’t really do anything different to its peers, but it packages it in such a bizarre bundle that I think it deserves your attention.
You play as the aforementioned teen, a pop punk prodigy who’s been turned into a shuffling corpse at the end of the world.
When he stumbles upon the frozen body of a beauty named Julia, he flushes himself down a toilet to take on an evil deity named KOM, all with the ambition of bringing her back to life.
The game’s opening hours are overstuffed with exposition, and I think the dev could have used a less heavy hand here, as I suspect it’s going to turn people off.
But effectively this is a run-based action game, where each jaunt into the khazi sees you work your way through “layers”, pummelling enemies pulled from various different fantasy realms.
There are werewolves, cyclops, and harpies – to name just a few – many of which can be “eaten” by Davy so he can “absorb” their powers.
My initial impressions of the combat were negative, because it’s all a bit loose in Davy’s standard form. But once you start masquerading as many of the abovementioned monsters, it feels a lot better. (Although it still lacks the punch of a proper character action game.)
The more enemies you pummel, the quicker you’ll be able to level up, giving the game that “one more go” factor which the best roguelites thrive on.
I’d argue the title has a little too much going on, but there’s no doubt it’s constantly layering in mechanics which make subsequent runs that bit more manageable.
For example, you can “buy” perks from a burger vendor named Bessie using in-game currency, which expands your available build options in each run.
You can also find body parts in some layers, which come with statistical attributes and even some active gameplay modifiers. For example, one “head part” I discovered surrounded Davy with landmines when he got knocked to the floor – useful.
The game loop is about optimising Davy’s loadout for success, then.
As with many roguelites, like Saros or Hades , sometimes your success will depend entirely on luck and the perks you randomly unlock during your run.
I found the game a bit restrictive at times; early on in the campaign, it’ll constantly stop your momentum when you beat a boss, taking you back to the beginning to lob fresh exposition and systems in your direction
But I did ultimately settle into a steady rhythm here, because you’re constantly edging forward, increasing Davy’s power and his capabilities in combat.
I was quite surprised by the overall attention to small details. For example, when in the real world, the protagonist shuffles like a zombie – but you quickly unlock a Roomba which allows you to zip about, minimising frustration.
The game’s hub area is presented like a mall, and it’s absolutely bursting with pop culture references, like the names of the families from Romeo & Juliet which adorn some of the shop signs.
Its presentation is chaotic, with random “sticker bombing” occurring all over the screen. I love how as you unlock perks, they slowly layer up around the user interface in the top-right corner.
But it’s absolutely an acquired taste; if you’re not into doodle art and the homemade “punkzine” aesthetic, then it won’t land for you.
And the sense of humour toes a fine line between juvenile and straight-up surreal, with certain characters suddenly breaking out into musical numbers and all sorts of other oddities.
It worked for me, but I’ll readily admit this is a vibe I’ve always quite liked. Your mileage will absolutely vary.
I personally found the allure of the next strange scenario motivating enough to keep me pushing forward, because the game does ultimately get repetitive once you get into the meat and potatoes of it.
Like any roguelite, the majority of your playtime here will be spent whaling away on fodder enemies, and I found some types – like the flying harpies – a little irritating to deal with. It’s not the end of the world, but I do think Davy’s movement could have been tightened up a touch.
But if your gaming diet is founded on oddities like No More Heroes , then I do think you’ll get a kick out of this barmy debut effort.
At a time when many games can start to look and feel a bit samey, the kitchen sink approach here helps this particular title to stand out – even if it’s garish and bordering on ugly in places as a result.
Stupid Never Dies is an acquired taste, but its lurid aesthetic and unhinged storytelling at least gives it a bit of personality in a crowded market.
As a roguelite, it’s got a good power curve and enough mechanics to keep you coming back, although sometimes its systems and narrative can get in the way of letting you just play the game.
It’s difficult to stand out in this genre these days, but GPTRACK50 has done enough here to deliver an experience that feels fresh – despite its underlying similarities to other titles in the genre.
As the Editor of Push Square, Sammy has over 15 years of experience analysing the world of PlayStation, from PS3 through PS5 and everything in between. He’s an expert on PS Studios and industry matters, as well as sports games and simulators. He also enjoys RPGs when he has the time to dedicate to them, and is a bit of a gacha whale.
Happy to answer any questions about the game if you have any. Let me know!
The game title sounds like the perfect summary of PlayStation’s recent business decisions.
I’ll definitely get this at some point, but with so many games currently coming out… well. I don’t really have time for it right now.
I thought the game had that PS2 and Suda51 vibe to it. It looks like a fun time.
@ShadowRJ I was going to make that joke, but you beat me to it.
Wait you're telling me Suda51 isnt behind this game?
Already had it pre-ordered for the 48-hour early access, going to start it in a bit. Since the reveal it just clicked with me, and the demo and knowing SEGA was supporting it with publishing made it an instant buy. I will always support (as long as the bank account allows it) this kind of games with my wallet.
Maybe on a deep sale....WAY too much out right now. No one should be releasing games at this time! But if that were true, then there would be no competition....forgot what I said, EVERYONE RELEASE AN AWESOME GAME RIGHT NOW! Oh no, now we're back where we started...
Huh. I can't seem to find the "Not Like Other Girls" section on PSN. Halp.
@Nepp67 Haha, it definitely looks/feels like one of his games.
Got a hard copy on pre-order, I'm looking forward to it! This is definitely my style of game, as the demo made abundantly clear.
The demo already made me expect it to review the way it did. Seems like a fine, goofy romp but rn we're loaded with goodass games - from capcom in particular, funnily enough - and I doubt I'll get much more beyond OoT this year anymore. Still got Onimusha on the back burner and I kind of want to try to squeeze in a hard mode run of FF7R, finally, before the final game in that trilogy.
Don't really know who the target audience is, because the age group it might appeal to is too used to a free to play model and are very likely not playing on a console anyways.

articles.title_orig: UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
articles.title_zh: UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — U.K. fighter jets will be sent to aid Saudi Arabia in defending itself against attacks on critical energy and civilian infrastructure by the Houthis.
The Iranian-backed Islamist militia group, based in civil war-hit Yemen, has been launching ballistic missile strikes on Saudi Arabia for the past few weeks, successfully hitting three airports earlier this month.
The Ministry of Defence announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighters will be deployed to the Gulf Kingdom — while stressing that they will be only used in a defensive capacity.
U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the “continuing attacks” on the U.K.’s ally are “absolutely despicable.”
“The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” he added, referencing the attacks earlier this month that killed 14 people and injured hundreds more.
Streeting said that the fighter jets will be used to protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. The U.K. will also send an Atlas A400M aircraft, used to transport the equipment, as well as military advisers.
“This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” Streeting said.
The MoD argued that there is a link between the conflict in the Persian Gulf and the situation domestically in the U.K., pointing to disrupted energy supplies and a subsequent rise in the cost of living.
Since Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street in July he has offered more support to Saudi Arabia. In September, he agreed to a request for air-to-air refueling of the country’s jets.
Pressed Tuesday on whether the U.K. risked being sucked into the Saudi war with the Houthis, Burnham’s official spokesperson told reporters: “I don’t accept that characterization. Our support for Saudi Arabia is considered proportionate and focused on helping them defend themselves against relentless Houthi attacks.”
They added: “Regional instability can have a serious impact at home in the U.K. We’re clear it’s in the U.K.’s economic and security interests that the Houthis do not succeed, and our approach is about defending our people, our interests, and our allies.”

articles.title_orig: Antigravity just halved the price of its drone — by swapping its headset for wristwatch control
articles.title_zh: Antigravity just halved the price of its drone — by swapping its headset for wristwatch control
articles.content_orig:
Drone company Antigravity has launched new wrist- and finger-mounted remote controls for the Antigravity A1, allowing users to fly the 360-degree video drone without a headset . These more subtle control options mean users can now capture some very impressive selfie footage without goggles getting in the way.
Introduced in December last year, the Antigravity A1 aims to offer high-quality 360-degree video while still being easy for amateurs to pilot. At the time, the A1 could only be flown using Antigravity's Vision goggles and Grip controller, both of which came bundled with the drone.
However, while this control scheme offered an immersive and intuitive experience, the Vision goggles prevented drone pilots from seeing what was around them. This limited A1 users' situational awareness, meaning they needed a spotter to watch both the drone and its pilot when flying. The FAA requires recreational pilots to maintain visual line of sight with their drone, or else have an observer watching who is in direct communication with them.
The Antigravity A1 Follow Me Bundle has now addressed such limitations with its Watch and Ring Remotes, new control options that allow users to use their drone without the Vision goggles. This means Antigravity A1 users can film themselves without their faces obscured as well as fly it solo, making the drone much more versatile.
The Watch is the undisputed star of the Antigravity A1 Follow Me Bundle. Drone pilots can use the Watch's 1.72-inch touchscreen to manually control the A1, or capture quick cinematic shots by selecting from preset movements such as Arc Out and Spiral Ascent. They can also use it to circle a subject on the move with Orbit Follow, choosing between clockwise and counterclockwise.
In addition to this, the Watch Remote's arguably most useful function is its ability to easily set up the Antigravity A1's Deep Track feature, including to track the drone pilot themselves. Simply select a subject, and the A1 drone will automatically follow and film them as they move at a maximum pace of around 22.4 mph (11 m/s). Users can choose where the drone is in relation to their subject (behind, ahead, or to the sides), as well as its elevation, and adjust these settings during flight.
As such, the Watch is a great accessory if you want to capture hikes, cycling, skiing, or other adventures where you're on the move. All you need to do is set up tracking and let the Antigravity A1 take care of the filming while you monitor its flight. The 360-degree footage means you'll have plenty of framing options afterward as well.
Though the Watch can be used to operate the A1 on its own, the Ring must be used in conjunction with the Watch. After using the Watch to select a tracking subject, users can press and hold the Ring's single button to control the A1 drone with hand gestures. This new Drag-To-Fly feature allows you to move your arm up and down or left to right to move the drone in that direction, as well as rotate your arm toward or away from you to change its distance (though you can only move it along one plane at a time unless in Orbit Follow mode).
Mashable's first impressions found that the Ring Remote doesn't feel as easy or precise as the Watch's manual touchscreen sliders, and can get uncomfortable if you're constantly changing your drone's position. Still, users may find it handy for quick adjustments, and the Watch Remote alone makes the Follow Me Bundle an incredibly handy investment for Antigravity A1 owners.
Alongside the Watch and Ring remotes, the Follow Me Bundle also introduces new Full-Coverage Propeller Guards that can be snapped onto the A1's arms, fully encasing its four propellers in lightweight plastic cages. While the A1's obstacle avoidance system is intended to prevent any collisions, it's still reassuring to have that extra security for peace of mind.
The Propeller Guards do need to be detached and reattached every time you want to fly, and add some extra bulk you need to consider when carrying your A1 to your launch site. Fortunately, the Follow Me Bundle comes with a crossbody bag to help you keep things organized.
The Antigravity A1 Follow Me Bundle includes the A1 drone, and is available now for $799 through the Antigravity website and Best Buy. The Follow Me Accessory Kit without the A1 drone is $339.99, while the Full-Coverage Propeller Guards are $39.99. However, existing A1 owners can get a 20 percent discount on the Accessory Kit and Guards, bringing them down to $271.99 and $31.99, respectively.
